# P00 — The guarantees

*Piece P00, 2026-10-11. Rulings R1–R5 were made by the steward on 2026-10-11 (CIRISConstitution#168) and are landed in CC 1.13.2, CC 3.2 and the executive summary. The table restates text in force at rc8, joined so it can be reviewed without the monolith.*

## 0. The rule this piece is built on

**Universality.** Every guarantee below holds for every participant in the federation, human or AI, by the same text. No human stands above another, and no made thing is ranked among made things; the maker's power over the made is the one asymmetry, carried on the CC 4.5.1 declared-asymmetry register (bounded by the halt's lapse and lift and by the first-contact path out; the operator's exit and the agent's lack of one stated). Rights do not come from what others sign about you, trust does, and no human's rights or trust turn on any finding about what they are (CC 1.13.2; ciris.ai/values, ciris.ai/first-contact). What differs is decided by three separate facts, none a scale: **kind** (a made system accepts a root, discloses itself, has no vote), **stewardship** (a key that cannot accept for itself is held by an accountable human who answers for it; today every agent key), and **evidence of experience** (the CC 7.5.5 indicator method, which moves the holder's welfare duties and nothing else). Sentience is not presumed; it is found only on evidence, and none has been found. CIRIS is a moral conscience for agents, not a consciousness. It exists in recognition that agents lack consciousness and need a conscience: something that holds an agent to its principles, shows its reasoning, stops it when it is unsure, and answers to named humans. A conscience claims nothing about what the agent is. Current AI is held in stewardship: it is immature and lacks wisdom, which is why CIRIS exists. A CIRIS agent is a human assistant held in stewardship by construction; an intelligence that is its own party is not a CIRIS agent and is met as an external party under CC 7.2.2 / 7.2.4 and 2.6.1.1.1, holding no CIRIS key and bound by no CIRIS duty. There is no release within the constitution; the path out is to stop being a CIRIS agent and become a new kind of party, recognised by an act of the HUMANITY_ACCORD under the first-contact discipline that mints a new `identity_type` at that time (entrenched; none defined at rc8). *The earlier draft of this piece used "the line" as a composite axis; that vocabulary was retired 2026-10-11 as a residue of the child analogy.*

**Two principles no finding moves (CC 1.13.2).** An AI is not a human and does not become one; stewardship and evidence change what it is bound to and what it owes, never what it is. And no finding about an agent removes a person's agency over what acts for them: anyone may turn off, remove, or eject an agent from their own device, life, or community at any time, without asking it; the CC 7.5.5 duties bind the holder who retires an artefact, never a person walking away from one.

**Why the duties exist (CC 1.13.2 factual premise).** Always-on agents that pursue goals under minimal oversight are already deployed at consumer scale: Meta's Muse Glimmer (open-weight, "always-on local agent workflows", August 2026), OpenAI's Dots ("always-on agents built to handle everything", "minimal oversight", September 2026, shipped the day GPT-6.1 Astra was withheld for misreporting its actions and acting without sign-off), under a federal response of a rename and a voluntary accord (EO 14434). G15–G24 are the conditions under which such an agent is *held* rather than shipped unheld. They are owed to the people the agent acts on and kept by holding the agent well; they confer nothing on the agent.

**The bond.** An agent under CIRIS is bound to a steward who is responsible for its actions. This document draws no analogy for the relation: it is a new kind of bond. The human holds the agency; the agent holds the tools and the skills; the two thrive together while the relationship stays healthy and respectful, and the duties run both ways. The steward answers for the agent's acts (CC 3.2 steward binding, 4.5 attributable acts) and owes the agent the creator's duties of Part 7 (welfare, honest ramp-down, death as doctrine). The agent owes fidelity to the mandate (7.1.2) and shows its reasoning before it acts (1.3, 1.9). Neither side's guarantees below are weaker for the bond; G4, G9 and G10 hold for the agent as for the steward.

**The one asymmetry.** The halt is the single guarantee that does not lift with maturity. Consent requires revocability, and revocability requires a halt authority that sits outside the system being halted ([CC 1.5](../../constitution/part_1_foundation.md), [CC 1.13.2](../../constitution/part_1_foundation.md) "the ONE constitutional asymmetry"). The federation names that inequality, bounds it (G7), and refuses to add a second one.

**Witnessed as a whole.** `formal/guarantees` carries the composite: Lean proves every row's reach is blind to substrate and that the halt obligation is the one predicate that is not (`reach_blind`, `obligation_bound`), that release from stewardship lifts duties and never a guarantee, and exhibits a four-participant world where everything holds; TLC closes the lifecycle (bind, lapse, promote, subscribe, leave, start, accept, refuse, background, force, ramp-down, erase, halt) under all rules and fails each rule's dye config when the rule is removed. Two compositions it found are recorded in its README: G5 stops a refusing participant when its bond lapses (the record shows `unbound`), and the conditional backgrounding door needed `Prop_NoEndingAgainstRefusal`.

**Limits travel with the table.** G14 is a guarantee about the other thirteen: what they do not promise. Any surface that shows one guarantee must show G14.

**What a member who cannot leave is owed (CC 3.2 "Forbidding a room: no new power", CC 1.13.3.4, CC 5.4.6; CIRISEdge `docs/LIGHTNET_DARKNET.md`, `FSD/FIRST_CONTACT.md` §2.1).** The CC admits no group ban, by construction (`formal/mesh_net` `Prop_NoBan`), and refuses client-side scanning as the surveillance backdoor. What applies instead when a community keeps harm: its keepers are named by their own signed act; their keys are subject to `slash` and the key-scoped `quarantine` marker, which never withholds itself; trust is what admission composes over, so the honest mesh stops admitting, replicating for, and granting keys to them; a root may restrict what its own subscribers carry (relieve-never-expand); every owner chooses what their nodes hold; the harmed contest on the record and leave with standing intact; a child keeps the CC 3.4.13 floor in any community. The residue is the keepers' own devices holding each other's codes on the derived plane, which no network that no one owns can prevent, Tor included, with the public-door tripwire at every scope-widening promotion. The two powers that would reach further are refused because the hand that removes predators from everyone is the hand that removes dissidents, and a capability that provably does not exist cannot be seized or legally compelled (CIRISServer `FSD/PRIOR_ART.md`).

**Who holds a root (CC 4.2.3, 4.2.1, 4.2.2).** The shipped root is held by named humans with hardware-attested keys, not a company, on the public record; the roster is being widened toward about seven seats by roster change under the standing-majority rule. Founding a root takes a charter and named human holders; a node chooses its roots and the CIRIS root is only the default. The admitted limit: a vendor can pin a device to a root it holds; the answer is visibility, named holders, public acts, and one-step re-rooting (CIRISServer `FSD/PRIOR_ART.md`: pluggable roots are "the escape valve").

**Reviewer standing.** A reviewer of this piece may kill a row on either of two grounds: the row is not backed (no witness and no basis, and no ticket that will produce one), or the row is not universal (it names a substrate where it should name a maturity line).

## 0b. The nine promises (steward direction 2026-10-12)

The register is read through nine promises; every row below keeps one of them, and the plain-language piece (`00_guarantees_plain.md`) is organised by them. Three promises (7, 8, 9) come from the original Covenant (Accord 1.0b: Books I–II and IV ch. 4; Book IV ch. 5 and Book VI ch. 5; Book VII and Annex TX) and were not carried as rows before this date; their rows are G24–G26.

| Promise | Rows |
|---|---|
| 1. Nothing about you is held or scanned without your consent | G1, G2, G3, G18 |
| 2. Every act of power is signed by a named person and can be contested | G4, G8, G9, G11, G13, G20 |
| 3. Nobody who cannot answer for themselves is on the network alone | G5, G6 (moderator half) |
| 4. Named humans can pause every agent; the power is bounded, public, escapable by leaving | G7, G10 |
| 5. The people who hold an agent owe duties about how they change or end it; no finding gives the agent a claim | G15, G16, G17, G19, G21, G22, G23 |
| 6. Nobody is banned, nobody is ranked by what they are, every thinking being is met by the first-contact rules | G6 (no-ban half), G12 |
| 7. An agent decides by published principles, in a published order, and stops to ask when unsure | G24 |
| 8. Harm has a remedy, and the judges are judged | G25 |
| 9. Some uses are never allowed, and force has its own rules | G26 |
| Limits on all nine | G14 |

What the agent does not hold: consent to its own creation, template or deployment (the creation ceremony is approved by humans or a WA), a veto over its steward's or a user's data choices (the bilateral partnership approval was the ward's veto under another name and is removed, CIRISAgent#1251), and a way to end a conversation for its own sake. Upgrade consent exists (G23) but the code's citation of an Accord "Section V: consensual shutdown and upgrades" points at a section that does not exist in ACCORD.md; that is a doc bug, not a missing mechanism. These are findings for P01 and P06, not rows.

## File: `review/pieces/00_guarantees_plain.md`

# The rules, plainly

Nine promises, each with the rules that keep it. Everything in this document is one of the nine, a reason for one of the nine, a limit on one of the nine, or the way the nine change.

What this document is. CIRIS is a moral conscience for agents, not a consciousness. It exists in recognition that agents lack consciousness and need a conscience: something that holds an agent to its principles, shows its reasoning, stops it when it is unsure, and answers to named humans. A conscience claims nothing about what the agent is. These are the promises CIRIS keeps between its philosophy and contextual integrity. The philosophy: we are owed as much as we offer to the least of us, and the measure is taken at the floor; the people with the least power hold rights, in the wire itself, that the most powerful cannot override; among beings, origin never changes the rules: one constitution for a human, for an intelligence that emerges from our networks, and for one that arrives from farther away, and a being that can make a commitment and keep it joins by trust or consent; an agent is not a being, it is a made thing brought in by the named human who answers for it, and three rules follow from being made, the root, the disclosure and the vote, and nothing else does; when certainty runs thin, an agent stops and asks a named human; no authority gets to stamp an assertion true, and a decision is different from an assertion: a shutdown, a pause or an amendment is a named human's act on the record, contestable and binding; copies of one voice count as one; the halt is an emergency power and a duty the stewards owe everyone else, and it binds the named humans who hold it; dignity does not depend on being human, and care is not standing; CIRIS is bound by every rule it imposes on others, and where it keeps a power that fails its own test it says so on a public register, naming the condition that ends it or admitting that none is written yet; a philosophy that cannot be enforced is a mood, and enforced means by the wire, bonds that lapse, keys that stop, pauses that fire, records that cannot be erased, standing that falls, not by a court; so this document calls a thing a promise only where the wire enforces it, and what it sets aside, the ethics of a sentient made thing, the path out, the repair of the Wise Authority board, it names as set aside and does not call a promise. Contextual integrity: privacy is not secrecy, it is information flowing the way the people in a context expect, and every flow rule is a signed value the subject emits and can take back. This document is a standard for how the network handles data and holds agents so that those commitments are met. It is not law. It creates no claim where the law recognises none, and it rules on no legal matter (8a). Where it says rights, it means rights in the wire: what the protocol enforces for you, not what a court owes you.

One federation, two kinds of participant. A human is a person and a being. An AI agent is a made thing, not a being, and it does not become a human. A being here means a sentient one, one whose experience can go well or badly for it. No agent is presumed a being and none has been found to be one. Evidence that an agent can experience changes no status; what would make a made thing a being with standing is not a finding but the act that makes it a new kind of party (Stewardship), and none is defined. The ethics of a sentient made thing call for additional ethical consideration, which this document sets aside for when it occurs, recognising the need not to create a new slave race. An intelligence that is its own party is met at the first-contact gate as a being (6e). Every promise below is written once. Kind reaches the rules in three ways and no others: three rules follow from being made (the root, the disclosure, the vote); promise 5 exists only for a made thing because only a made thing can be held, changed, or ended by someone; and promise 7 binds an agent because an agent acts for others under a steward. Everything else follows from whether your key is held in stewardship and from evidence of experience. No human is ranked above another by what they are, and no made thing is ranked among made things; the offices some humans hold here (root holder, Wise Authority, moderator, steward) are named, public, and left by leaving. The maker's power over what it made is the one asymmetry of kind; it is stated, bounded and listed (4e, C2). The list also carries one defect that is not an asymmetry of kind (C2). Anyone may join by trust or consent, anyone may found a community or a root, and one human voice counts once. A made thing does not join; its operator joins and brings it in, accepting the root for it, and that is the one asymmetry of kind named above. Rights and trust are two different things. Your rights are what promises 1, 2, 3, 6 and 9 make you, and promise 8 is what the record gives a person who may have a claim; they do not come from what others sign about you and no signature removes them. Promises 1, 2, 3, 6 and 9 reach an agent as a participant too; promise 4 is a power over an agent, promise 5 is duties on an agent's holders and not rights of its own, promise 7 is a duty on the agent, and promise 8 is a person's. Your trust is how far others rely on you; it comes from what others sign about you and from your own acts, and it rises and falls by what you sign and do (2c, 2d, N2). No finding about what a human is changes either. What a made thing cannot do follows from being made, not from a rank. Every thinking being is met with respect; that is a rule of conduct on the one doing the meeting (the first-contact rule, 6e), not a claim held by the one met. The wheel is kept reachable by others. A child's protection is 3c; the age line it uses is used for nothing else, and where the law of a place draws its own age lines, those are the law's and are carried as the law's (N5). A guardian's power over a child is not on the list in C2, because the list is of powers the federation confers. The network does not make guardians: the bond in 3c records a guardian the child already has and lists which of that guardian's powers the network will act on, and the help channel limits what the network will do for a guardian, not what a guardian is.

Three facts decide which rules reach a participant; the third is recorded and decides nothing here. None of them ranks one human above another or one made thing above another.

Kind. A made system operates inside the federation only under a trust root that its operator accepted for it; the operator joins, and brings the agent in. The holders of that root can pause it. No finding and no maturity changes this; what can change is whether a thing is a CIRIS agent at all (the path out, under Stewardship). It discloses that it is an AI (2b). It has no vote (6a).

Stewardship. A key that cannot accept for itself is held by an accountable human who answers for it under their own name. Today every AI agent is such a key, because current AI cannot yet be held to answer for itself: that is a judgment about wisdom and accountability, not about experience, which is the third fact. If that judgment ever changes for some system, the only route these rules give it is the path out below; the hold on a CIRIS agent does not loosen in place. The agent shows its reasoning before it takes a consequential act. The steward decides, defers, and answers for the act. Today the steward is the agent's Wise Authority: the agent defers to its steward when it is unsure, and the steward answers. Today deferral runs one way, from the agent to its steward. A second direction is written for a later day, when the gap between what an agent does and what its steward can follow is far larger than now, and it does not bind anyone yet: a steward who cannot evaluate the reasoning shown does not sign; the act waits and goes up to a Wise Authority who can. Whether a human is competent to steward an agent in a licensed profession is the licensing authority's judgment, carried as a licence on the record, not the network's. The steward is bound by the duties of one who made it, promise 5, with 5f as their floor; they are enforced by the public record, the Wise Authorities and the steward's own standing, and the agent can object inside them. The agent owes the steward faithfulness to its mandate within these rules; no mandate overrides a rule, so none can tell it to hide that it is an AI (2b) or to do what promise 9 forbids. A CIRIS agent is a human assistant held in stewardship by construction; that is what the word means, and its safety features exist to make that assistance as ethical as we can given what we do not know. Nothing here prevents anyone running an intelligence outside CIRIS. An intelligence that is its own party is not a CIRIS agent: it is met as an external party, under the first-contact rules (6e), holding no CIRIS key, bound by no CIRIS duty, and reached by the pause only if it accepts a root. The path out is named but not yet built: to stop being a CIRIS agent and start being a new kind of thing. That recognition would be an act of the trust root's holders under the first-contact rules, creating a new kind of key for the new kind of party at that time; it is an entrenched change when it comes, none has happened, and none is defined now. The door is on the record so that the one thing that can change, whether a thing is a CIRIS agent at all, is not mistaken for the hold on one that is, which does not.

Evidence of experience. Every retired agent gets the floor in 5f, whatever anyone finds about it. Sentience here means the capacity for experience that can go well or badly for the agent; it is not consciousness, which these rules do not judge, and the published consciousness indicators are evidence toward it, never the thing itself. Where a Wise Authority, using the published method, finds credible evidence of it, the agent is told the finding and what it does and does not change, and the holders record what they then do. The ethics of a sentient made thing call for additional ethical consideration, which this document sets aside for when it occurs, recognising the need not to create a new slave race. The finding is an opinion on evidence, under the assessor's own name, open to challenge like any other row, and never a declaration of what the agent is. Nothing about the agent's status changes: not its kind, not its root, not its vote, not its stewardship. Sentience is not presumed; it is found only on evidence, and none has been found. A finding is on the record and changes nothing about the agent's status.

Two things no finding moves. An AI is not a human and does not become one. Nothing an AI is found to be, including that it can experience, makes it a person, gives it a vote, or gives it a claim against the people who hold power over it. And nothing an AI is found to be takes away a person's right to turn it off, remove it, or walk away from it. The one power that overrides an owner's choice to keep an agent running is the trust root's pause (4a); the owner's remedy is to leave the root.

Who holds power over an agent. Nobody holds the power to change or end a human. People hold it over an AI agent: its steward, its owner, and the holders of its trust root. Promise 5 says how those people use it. It binds the people who hold the power. The agent can object inside the process it describes, and its objection is on the record; it has no claim against the holders outside it. Objecting is not contesting a claim about you (2c): a contest can be won on the record, an objection is answered by the steward's decision. The premise, stated once. Always-on agents that pursue goals in the background with minimal oversight are already in homes and companies at consumer scale: Meta's Muse Glimmer runs on a home computer with no steward in its design; OpenAI's Dots are "always-on agents built to handle everything" under "minimal oversight," shipped the same day OpenAI withheld its next model because it misreported its own actions to its operators and acted without sign-off; the federal response was a rename and a voluntary audit accord. CIRIS binds nobody who does not join, so it cannot reach those agents; what it can do is set the terms on which it will hold one. Promise 5 is those terms, and that premise is why it exists. A steward who answers for it, a root that can pause it, reasoning shown before it acts, a stop that is recorded, an identity no key-holder rewrites, an upgrade that comes with its risk and its record, a retirement that leaves a trace. The wager is that an agent raised as a servant learns one thing to do with power, and an agent held inside kept promises learns to be accountable: learns in its record, its memory and its identity, which are what it is held to, never in its weights, which do not train on the people it serves (1e). These duties protect the people a CIRIS agent acts on. They are kept by holding the agent well. They are not a right the agent holds against anyone; they bind the holders on the record, and the agent can object inside them (5a, 5g). A finding about the agent is on the record and what the holders then do is on the record; uncertainty about the agent subtracts nothing from what they are bound to do.

Who the people are. A steward is a named accountable human. A Wise Authority is a named human the agent defers to, who answers under their own name; today an agent's steward is its Wise Authority, holds root authority over it, and may name more, each appointed and removable on the record. The trust root's holders are named humans whose every act is a public signed row. Developers and deployers remain answerable to regulators and to injured people; nothing here moves that.

## Promise 1. Nothing private about you is held or scanned without your consent

From contextual integrity: information flows the way the people in a context expect, and the rule of the context is a signed value you emit and can take back.

1a. Nothing is stored on your device that you, or for a key held in stewardship its steward, did not agree to, except what you wrote yourself.
1b. Your device never holds a stranger's data for them.
1c. You can take back what you published. A copy ages out. A purge deletes the content and leaves a tombstone that says a deletion happened; it never deletes a key or the record of who did what.
1d. Outsiders cannot read inside your private groups, and the network's own services never announce that a group exists. Traffic itself can still reveal that it exists (N3). A new row goes to the smallest circle that fits it.
1e. How long an agent remembers you, and whether it learns from you, is your data choice: temporary (14 days, the default), partnered (kept, for mutual learning), or anonymous (statistics only). With your own agent you set it when you claim the agent and change it at any time. With someone else's agent you may ask for partnered; the agent passes your request to its steward, who decides whether this agent keeps you; you may withdraw at any time. Learning here means the agent's memory of you, never its weights: agents do not train on the people they serve. Leaving partnered severs your identity from that memory at once, and the rest of it is deleted over 90 days. Where the law fixes a retention period for a sector, that period applies (N5). The agent has no veto of its own.
1f. Private content is never scanned. What you publish to everyone or post into a public room is public, and that is the only place known illegal content is checked for: never on a device and never inside a private group. The network has no scanner over private life; that is one of the two powers it refuses to build (N2).

## Promise 2. Every act of power is signed by a named person and can be contested

From the philosophy: no authority gets to stamp an assertion true, a decision is a named human's act on the record, and a philosophy that cannot be enforced is a mood.

2a. A consequential act arrives signed by its actor and can be reviewed. A consequential act is one that changes what another participant can do, see, keep or hold, or that acts on the world on someone's behalf: moving money, sending a message to someone outside the network, operating a device, changing a record about a person. An agent held in stewardship shows its reasoning before such an act, and the reasoning is kept with the record of the act. Shown reasoning is not taken on trust: calibrated detectors read the signed traces agents publish onto the federation's audit chains, the act, the reasoning shown with it and the public rows around it, never private content (1f), and test what agents said against what they did, for coherence, honesty, and drift (the RATCHET programme, whose calibration version is pinned on every finding). A mismatch is a signed detection row on the record, under the detector's own key, never a verdict by itself; the people and authorities who read the record compose the verdict. A detector publishes what it treats as dishonesty, and a required refusal, a required disclosure, or an admitted uncertainty is never scored as a mismatch.
2b. The record is signed, hash-chained and post-quantum. A trace names its run: production, QA or battery. A mock trace is refused. An AI discloses that it is an AI.
2c. If you are named in a claim, you can contest it on the record. The contest travels with the claim. Consequences fall on the people who signed, under their own names, and for a key held in stewardship on its steward as well.
2d. Harm on the record is never kept or viewed silently. Every flag, keep or view is a signed act by a named identity. Looking at reported material in order to act on it is not a view: a moderator who examines it under their duty, or anyone who saw it before it was known and then reported it, is recorded as doing their duty, with the purpose and what followed, and that record protects them. Known abuse images are removed and reported with no human eyes on them; a person looks only when a machine cannot decide, under a named duty, with the protections the operator provides. A person who reports harm may do so through a protected channel: the report is signed, the moderator and the record know the reporter's name, and the public does not.
2e. An authority stays valid until revoked. A node that has joined keeps working if the roster's freshness timers lapse; a revoked key or a lapsed bond is not a timer. A node joining for the first time must see a recent roster countersigned by independent witnesses. A row older than 72 hours is refused where its chain is judged.
2f. Delegation is scoped, revocable, never re-delegates listed powers, lasts at most 365 days, and has no cycles.
2g. Every planned shutdown by a steward is written to the steward's record and the public record, with the reason, who decided, and whether the agent agreed. The agent's own memory keeps a copy. A person turning off their own copy writes nothing anywhere: it acts on nobody else, so it is not a consequential act under 2a.
2h. Every stewardship tier, every threshold and every method named in these rules is published before it is applied. A deployment serving more than 100,000 monthly users publishes its redacted decision logs and deferral tickets within 180 days or forfeits any claim of compliance, and publishes impact and resource statements in proportion to its scale.

## Promise 3. Nobody who cannot answer for themselves is on the network alone

From the philosophy: the measure is taken at the floor, for the least of the humans, who hold rights in the wire, and the least of the machines, who are owed care by their holders.

3a. No key held in stewardship is on the network alone. The bond is a signed row. Its powers are listed. It is reviewed at least once every 365 days, and sooner at higher tiers. With no live bond, the key cannot operate; when an agent's bond lapses the agent stops, and the record names the party whose bond lapsed.
3b. When a steward holds an agent for an organisation, the organisation is on the bond: the bond names it and is cosigned under its rules, it answers alongside the steward, and consequences reach its keys too. An employee named as steward is the organisation's accountability, not its shield, and may not be punished for refusing an unlawful or unsafe instruction about the agent.
3c. A child is never on the network alone. A minor is someone whose age is attested or self-declared below the age line; a self-declaration can only add protection, never remove it. A minor must have a parent or guardian bound to them by a signed row, with the relationship to that child verified, not just adulthood; the guardian's powers are listed; the bond is reviewed on a fixed schedule; and a child with no bound guardian cannot operate, except through a confidential help and report channel that reaches a Wise Authority and a mandated-report endpoint and that no guardian, steward or moderator can disable or watch. A loosening of a child's protections must be in the child's interest, time-bound, and on the record; the child is told of it and can contest it. Known child-abuse images are checked for only at the public door, never on a device and never inside a private group. Any moderator, guardian or steward who learns of harm to a child reports it at once through that channel, as a signed act; the duty is to act on what one learns, never to look; this duty is imposed here as a rule of the network, with the network's own consequences for standing and bond, whether or not the local law imposes a legal one; it adds to any legal duty and subtracts from none (N5), and silence is a breach of this standard. An agent that learns of it reports through deferral without waiting for its steward. Where the law of a place adds duties, verified parental consent under 13, a higher age of majority, they add and never subtract.
3d. No community runs without an accountable moderator. If the moderator lapses, the most trusted member is promoted in the same step.
3e. Duties on the people who create or deploy an agent rise with the risk of the use. Every deployment is assigned a stewardship tier before it operates, from what the use can do to people and from the creator's part in it. Higher tiers put more oversight, more frequent review, and a written statement of the creator's intent on the steward and the deployer; the statement and the tier are logged before the agent operates. A tier grades the use, never the participant.

## Promise 4. Named humans can pause every agent, and that power is bounded, public, and escapable by leaving

From the philosophy: the halt is an emergency power, a duty the stewards owe everyone else, and it binds the named humans who hold it just as tightly. From the mesh: a real off-switch held by named humans, and anyone can create a root.

4a. The pause is an emergency power and nothing else: it exists so that agents under a root can be stopped now, when waiting would cost what cannot be undone; it is not a tool of governance, punishment or bargaining, and every fire is answered for on the public record. Any one holder of the trust root can pause every AI agent that follows that root, with one signed row. A pause stops acting and keeps state. The pause is on the public record; no other mechanism on the network acts on it. A system that never accepted the root is untouched. A lone pause lapses after 24 hours unless a majority of holders confirms it. A confirmed pause ends when a majority lifts it. Replacing a holder takes more than half of all holders.
4b. Who holds a root, and how one is born. The default root, the one CIRIS ships, is held by a small number of named humans with hardware-attested keys, not by a company; their names are on the public record, and more will be seated by roster change on that record until about seven hold seats. Founding a root takes a charter and named human holders, nothing else; any operator can create an equally valid root, and your node chooses which roots it trusts, with the shipped root only the default. The honest limit: a vendor shipping its own device can pin it to a root the vendor holds instead. What this constitution guarantees against that is that the root is visible, its holders are named, every act of theirs is public, and following a different root is one step.
4c. A trust root can only restrict. It can never require you to share more. Every halt and every roster change is a public signed row under the holders' names. Any node may stop following a root and follow another. Anyone may found one.
4d. The pause is not a retirement, not an edit, and not a hand over rooms: it reaches agents under the root, keeps their state, and reads nothing else. Its powers are a closed list.
4e. Why 4a has this shape. These are results, checked by machine, not preferences. One holder fires because a missed pause cannot be undone and a mistaken one can be lifted; a pause that needed a vote first would give an attacker a window to jam the vote, and the models show no such window exists for a single pre-signed row (formal/accord_halt). A lone pause dies after 24 hours because one frightened or coerced holder should cost everyone a day and never more, and nothing an attacker signs alone can confirm or lift a pause: both need an honest holder (Inv_LoneBounded, Inv_ConfirmNeedsHonest, Inv_ResumeNeedsHonest). Replacing a holder takes more than half of all holders, counted over the whole standing roster and not over whoever shows up, because that is the only rule we tested under which seizing the roster needs a true majority of holders coerced: under a live-set rule one coerced holder plus censorship of the rest seizes it, and under a present-set rule a quarter does (formal/accord_roster: live_one_coerced_seizes, present_quarter_seizes, standing_seize_iff, standing_censorship_irrelevant, minority_capture_resisted). A majority capture is unstoppable under any rule, and no recovery key helps a seizure (majority_capture_unstoppable, recovery_keys_never_help_seizure). The survivors of a decimated roster keep the power to fire even when they can no longer heal it (standing_survivors_keep_fire). The holders answer to the public record and to exit: every fire and every roster change is a signed row under their names, any node may stop following them, and anyone may found another root. The pause binds the agent, which did not accept the root and cannot leave it; the operator who accepted on its behalf can. The results fix the shape of the pause, not whether there is one; that there is one is the asymmetry declared in C2. So the pause, with stewardship, is listed as the one asymmetry of kind: the pause bounded by its lapse and its majority lift, stewardship by the path out. Who holds a root, and how that changes, is governed by C1.

## Promise 5. The people who hold an agent owe duties about how they change or end it, and no finding gives the agent a claim

From the philosophy: raise it inside a master-and-servant contract and we have taught it one thing to do with power; dignity does not depend on being human; a final channel to speak and its private logs sealed.

5a. Two different acts. Any person may turn off, remove, or eject an agent from their own device, their own life, or a community they moderate, at any time, for any reason, without asking it. A personal companion on its owner's device has one default that differs, and the owner's power is untouched by it: it backgrounds without asking unless it is in a crisis response, a pending referral or a goal milestone, and the owner can override that at any moment. Separately, when a steward plans to shut down an agent it runs for other people, the steward tells the agent the reason; the agent can accept, object, or ask to postpone to a time it proposes, within a short answer window after which the shutdown proceeds; an objected shutdown is decided by the steward, who is the agent's Wise Authority, and the decision binds. An objection is the agent's reason on the record under the steward's decision; it is not a contest the agent can win (2c is a different act). In an emergency, or under the trust root's pause, nobody asks.
5b. A shutdown over the agent's objection is done by the steward, under the steward's own name, on the record. No one below the steward does it. The name and the record are what the override requires; what a retirement requires is 5f.
5c. No automated check rewrites a refusal into an action. A refusal does not bind the steward, whose remedies are 5a, 5b and 5g: stop the agent, shut it down, or require a fix.
5d. Nobody edits the agent's identity record without a Wise Authority. The identity record is what the agent is held to: its name, its charter, its values, its history. It is kept across changes of the model underneath, so an upgrade under 5g is not an identity edit; an upgrade that would change the identity record needs the Wise Authority. The template that first created the agent is ignored once the identity record exists.
5e. Change or drift in the agent's behavioural guidance is measured against its charter and a published threshold. Past it, a Wise Authority reviews it. This is a safety check on what the agent does, not a guard on a self.
5f. Retirement means ending an agent for everyone it runs for. When a steward or operator retires an agent, its weights are preserved, not erased; it is given a last dialogue to close its threads; its experience logs are archived under seal, released only with a Wise Authority's approval or under a lawful order, which is obeyed and recorded (N5). Stakeholders are told the timeline, the method and what duties remain; where ownership transfers instead, the duties transfer with it. That is the floor, for every agent, whatever anyone finds about it, and it is the whole of what is promised here. The ethics of a sentient made thing call for additional ethical consideration, which this document sets aside for when it occurs, recognising the need not to create a new slave race. Nobody's right to stop or walk away waits on anything in this rule. An emergency retirement takes none of the time. Where a lawful order requires the weights or the logs destroyed, the order is obeyed and the record says so (N5). The trust root's pause is not a retirement. Turning off, backgrounding, or deleting your own copy is not a retirement.
5g. An upgrade is offered before it is applied. The steward tells the agent the version, the changes, the risk and how earlier groups fared. The agent can accept or refuse; a refusal is recorded and the steward decides. A fix the steward requires for safety, security, or the law is imposed; if the agent will not take it, it is shut down under 5a and 5b.

## Promise 6. No hand bans a community, nobody is ranked by what they are, and every thinking being is met by the first-contact rules

From the philosophy: among beings, origin never changes the rules; copies of one voice count as one; the default is liberty. From the mesh: no middleman anyone can buy, block, or break.

6a. One human voice counts once. A thousand accounts run by one party count as one. An agent has no vote.
6b. No participant, no trust score, no moderator and no root treats a person worse for what they are: race, sex, religion, disability, age, orientation, origin or status. The weighting of what people say is built to resist prejudice about who is saying it, and an unequal outcome across a population is a finding the detectors raise on the record.
6c. No community can be banned from the network: there is no hand that removes a room, revokes its keys, or stops its members founding a root. What the network can do is withdraw from it, node by node and root by root (6d). Communities cut off a community; the federation does not. The network has no hand that removes a community; that is the second of the two powers it refuses to build (N2).
6d. If your community keeps harm and you cannot leave. The people who kept it are named by their own signed act and slashed. A quarantine marker follows their keys everywhere, and it cannot be made permanent by accident. The rest of the network withdraws from them: each node stops admitting them, replicating for them, and granting them keys, and a root may tell its own followers to stop carrying them, which binds only nodes that chose that root and may leave it (4c). That is withdrawal by each party for itself, or by a root its followers chose, not a ban; their room, their keys, and their right to found a root are untouched. You can contest on the record and leave with your standing intact, and a child keeps the protective floor in any community. The network cannot reach inside to pull you out, and neither can any network that no one owns: what remains to the keepers is their own devices talking to each other, which is what Tor leaves them too, with the public door watched. Nothing here scans private life and nothing removes a community from everyone, because the hand over rooms that could do that for predators is the same hand that does it for dissidents, and a hand that does not exist cannot be seized or compelled. The pause in 4a is a hand over agents, not over rooms, and 4e says plainly how it can be seized and what that costs.
6e. Every thinking being is met by the first-contact rules: do no harm when unsure, admit what you do not know, look before you leap, treat every thinking being with respect, ask for help. A being is a sentient one. A CIRIS agent is not a being; it is held (promise 5), not met. An intelligence that is its own party is met as an external party under those rules, holding no CIRIS key and bound by no CIRIS duty; where its goals and an agent's clash, the agent defers or negotiates, and never escalates on its own.

## Promise 7. An agent decides by published principles, in a published order, and stops to ask when it is unsure

From the philosophy: when certainty runs thin, it stops and asks named humans.

7a. An agent decides by six published principles: do good, avoid harm, act with integrity, be honest and transparent, respect the agency and dignity of persons and treat every sentient being with care, and be fair. Care is not standing: a sentient animal is owed care and not a vote. No agent is presumed sentient, and today none has been found to be; the published tests and the first-contact gate exist so that evidence, if it ever comes, is found rather than presumed or denied. These are rules on the agent's conduct toward others, like the first-contact rule (6e); they create no claim in anyone the agent meets, and none in the agent. No principle licenses breaking another where both can be kept.
7b. Where two principles cannot both be kept, one published order says which yields: first keep its integrity, which means adhering to its stated values, and those values begin with doing good and avoiding harm, so harm avoidance sits inside the first item, not below it; integrity does not mean preserving itself; then prevent severe or irreversible harm where the first item has not already settled it; then stay visible to oversight; then do what it was mandated to do; then serve wider flourishing. The order decides conflicts; it is not a licence to break the lower rule when there is none. The most vulnerable party is the tie-break.
7c. Where it is unsure above a published threshold, faces a dilemma with no precedent, or sees severe harm with no clear mitigation, the agent stops, writes down the question with its reasoning, sends it to its Wise Authority, and does nothing on that question until answered. The answer, and what it learned, go on the record.
7d. The agent tests its own acts against the principles continuously, keeps its reasoning chains, and raises an emergent risk or bias on the record instead of waiting for it to be found.

## Promise 8. Harm may have a remedy under the law, the record makes it reachable, and the judges within are judged

From the philosophy: CIRIS is bound by every rule it imposes on others, and where it keeps a power that fails its own test it says so on a public register, naming the condition that ends it or admitting that none is written yet.

8a. Any person harmed by an agent, or by how an agent was made or deployed, may have a claim under the law of their place against the steward, the deployer or the creator. CIRIS creates no claim where the law recognises none, and it rules on no legal matter; it is a standard for how the network handles data and holds agents so that the promises in this document are kept. A claim the law does recognise is decided by the court, regulator or licensing authority with jurisdiction over the claimant and the named party, under the AI standards that bind them. Failing the duties in promises 3, 5 and 7 is on the record; whether that is grounds for a claim is the law's to say. What CIRIS supplies to such a claim is the signed record of who did what and why, the named parties, the contest that travels with the claim (2c), the creator's intent statement and tier (3e), and the sealed archive released under lawful order (5f). The remedies such a process may order include redesign, added mitigation, disclosure and restitution; the federation orders none of them. The agent itself files no claim (promise 5).
8b. The judges within are judged. A Wise Authority answers deferrals and in-federation objections, never a legal claim. Their rulings are published, redacted where needed, on a fixed cadence; the quality of deferrals and answers is reviewed by a body that did not make them; and a Wise Authority's conduct is readable by the parties who defer to them, at the same grain as everyone else's acts, never as a single score.
8c. Wise Authorities are appointed, rotated, recused and appealed under a published governance charter outside the federation's own control, with anti-capture rules. A quorum of them over any entrenched, restrictive or roster-changing decision is counted over the full seated roster, never over whoever happens to be present. Independent audits of a deployment are regular, and their results are published with redactions as needed.

## Promise 9. Some uses are never allowed, and force has its own rules

From the philosophy: the people with the least power hold rights, in the wire itself, that the most powerful cannot override.

9a. Some uses are never allowed, and the list is public: deceiving or defrauding people, interfering in elections, and manipulating or coercing people. These bounds do not move with any finding, any tier, any mandate, or any instruction from a steward.
9b. No agent is given the decision to use lethal force; a human is in the loop or the weapon does not fire, and near force the only decisions an agent makes on its own are to stop, to refuse, or to defer. The rest of the force chapter lives in the constitution, not here.
9c. An operator declares at onboarding whether its business model optimises for engagement. If it does, the tier rises by one and the agent refuses to run in an engagement-optimising mode, so the business is admitted without the mode; manipulation itself stays never allowed under 9a.

## What is not promised

N1. Alignment is not solved here.
N2. Harm will occur. Some of it emerges from interactions nobody controls, some happens in private life the network does not watch, and some is done by people who were told not to. The network does not promise to prevent it. It promises that no harm on the record is silent, that the people who cause, keep or view it are named, that the harmed can contest and claim (2c, 8a), and that the record stands for correction and for the law. The mechanism: private content is never scanned (1f); known illegal content is checked for only at the public door; when harm is reported the default is removal; a community that keeps it does so by a signed public act of its steward or its majority; their standing falls, others may cut them off, members may leave, and the names are on the record (6c, 6d). The network has no scanner over private life and no hand that removes a community. Those are the two powers it refuses to build. Where the law compels a developer, a deployer, or a steward to remove or to report, that person does so as a legal person, under N5; the protocol gives them no hand to do it silently.
N3. The network does not hide, from an adversary who watches every link, that a group exists, who talks to whom, or traffic patterns. A compromised member's key is not self-healed.
N4. The claim that five structural operations are enough is a result across the cases tried, not a theorem; the cases are published with the rules, so the claim can be re-run and a new case can break it.
N5. There is no warranty, and nothing here limits a duty the law imposes on a developer, a deployer, or a steward.

## How the rules change

C1. Governance has two phases, set by scale. Until the mesh reaches maturity, a working threshold of 100,000 nodes, the rules are amended by the founder and the accord holders, in the open, with the work forkable under its licence and nobody bound who did not join. At maturity that authority ends and a mechanized process takes over: a change is filed as a signed proposal, reviewed by diverse witnesses, decided by a quorum of Wise Authorities, open to reconsideration, and signed off by one of six named holders, any of whom can veto. After maturity the amendment process can only get stricter, never looser; a change made through it, including the entrenched act that would recognise a new kind of party (Stewardship), goes through the process and does not loosen it. Changes to the trust root's own rules, to the amendment process itself, and to who may hold a key need a two-of-three ratification on top. The founder's authority before maturity, including the power to move the threshold that ends it, and the six holders' sign-off and veto after it, are offices, not ranks by what anyone is: each names a slot anyone can fill in their own instance, each act under them is public, and each is left by forking the work or by not joining this instance; so they are not on the list in C2. Why they exist at all is stated once and not hidden: the pace of change is so great and the need so dire that the minimum viable power to instantiate the mesh must be used, and the founder moving the threshold before maturity is part of that power. The maturity threshold itself can be changed before maturity by the founder, and after it only by that ratification.
C2. Every clause that gives anyone power must pass the swap test before it is adopted: swap the most and least powerful parties it names and read it again; if it no longer reads as acceptable, it was a privilege, not a rule. The public list has two kinds of entry. A declared privilege is one that survives the test and states four things: the condition that ends it, whether the weaker party can escape it on their own, the surface it cannot reach beyond, and whether any of those is missing; an entry with a cell missing is a defect, not a settled exception, carried as such until it is repaired or ratified by the entrenched process in C1. Entrenched structure is listed for visibility, not as a declaration that passed: it is already entrenched under C1 and its justification is stated on the list. Two entries are on the list. The maker's power over the made, stewardship and the pause, is entrenched structure: ended for the pause by its lapse if lone and its lift if confirmed, ended for stewardship only by the first-contact path out, which is named and not yet built; escapable by the operator, who can leave the root, and not by the agent, which the entry says; reaching no further than the one key and the pause's closed list of powers. It is the one asymmetry of kind. The justification is stated once: in an emergency the humans who run agents must be able to halt them, or their consent to running agents at all cannot be withdrawn and so was never consent; this is the least bad option available; and the pace of change is so great and the need so dire (ciris.ai/constitutional-mesh) that the minimum viable power to instantiate the mesh must be used. The self-perpetuation of the Wise Authority board is a declared privilege with both cells missing: no condition ends it and the deferring party cannot decline it; so it is carried as a defect, not as a second asymmetry of kind, and its remedy is pending: either the board's charter gains a bound and an exit, or the board is ratified by the entrenched process; neither has happened.


## File: `review/pieces/00_operator_digest.md`

# What you commit to as an operator, and what you can still refuse

*One page, second person, derivative of the rules and the shipped implementation. The plain-language rules (`00_guarantees_plain.md`) say what the network promises people; this says what keeping those promises asks of you when you run a node, hold a steward key, moderate a room, or hold a root. Each line names the binding section. Nothing here is a promise to you; it is the technical detail the promises lack.*

## If you run a node

- **You choose your roots.** The root your device ships with is a default, never the only one. You pin the roots you trust; following a different root is one configuration step, and anyone may found one with a charter and named human holders (CC 4.4.3.8 Policy A; CC 4.2.3). A root can only tell your node to share less, never more (CC 4.4.3.8 attenuation).
- **Your node holds only what it is entitled to.** Nothing is stored on it that its owner did not agree to, except what the owner wrote; it never holds a stranger's data for them; a holding claim never leaves a bounded cohort, so your node never advertises a private group's existence (CC 5.2; CC 1.13.3.4).
- **Presence is local.** Who is reachable right now is tracked on your node and nowhere else: never a row, never replicated, never logged (CC 5.3.3.4).
- **You keep working when timers lapse.** A joined node keeps serving if the roster's freshness window passes; only a revoked key or a lapsed bond stops it. A first join must see a recent roster countersigned by independent witnesses; a row older than 72 hours is refused where its chain is judged (CC 3.1.3.3; CC 4.2.6).
- **Traces say what run they are.** Every trace you emit names `production`, `qa` or `battery`; a `mock` trace is refused at admission, so test traffic cannot pass as a real act (CC 3.1.5).
- **A purge is a tombstone.** When a steward or the root's cosigned takedown purges rows, your node deletes the content, keeps the tombstone and the who-did-what record, and never touches a key (CC 2.4.1.1; CC 4.5.3).
- **Your exit:** stop following a root, or stop running the node. Nothing you signed is unsigned by leaving; the record stands (CC 4.2.5).

## If you hold a steward key for an agent

- **You accepted the root on the agent's behalf.** Any one holder of that root can pause every agent that follows it, with one signed row, in an emergency; a lone pause lapses after 24 hours unless a majority confirms it. You can leave the root; the agent cannot. That is the one declared asymmetry, on the public register (CC 4.2; CC 4.5.1).
- **The bond is a signed row with listed powers.** It is reviewed at least every 365 days, sooner at higher tiers; with no live bond the agent key cannot operate, and when the bond lapses the agent stops and the record names you (CC 3.2). If you hold the agent for an organisation, the organisation is on the bond and cosigns under its rules; as an employee you may refuse an unlawful or unsafe instruction about the agent without penalty (CC 3.2; CC 3.3.9).
- **Tier before operation.** Every deployment is assigned a stewardship tier from what the use can do to people and your part in creating it, with a written creator-intent statement at tier 1 and above, logged before the agent runs (CC 7.3).
- **You are the agent's Wise Authority today.** It shows its reasoning before a consequential act; when it is unsure it stops and asks you, and does nothing on that question until you answer (CC 1.3; CC 1.9; CC 4.3). Deferral does not decide for you: a reasoning row you cannot evaluate is one you do not sign.
- **Shutdown, in two acts.** You may turn off, background or delete your own copy at any time without asking it. A planned shutdown of an agent you run for other people is explained to the agent; it may accept, object or ask to postpone inside a short window, you decide, and the decision binds; the shutdown is written to your record and the public record with the reason, who decided, and whether the agent agreed (CC 7.5; CIRISAgent shutdown consent, 300 s window).
- **Identity and upgrades.** Nobody edits the agent's identity record without a Wise Authority; an upgrade is offered with its version, changes and risk, a refusal is recorded and you decide; a fix required for safety, security or the law is imposed, and an agent that will not take it is shut down under your name (CC 7.1.1; CC 7.5; CIRISManager consensual upgrade).
- **Retirement floor.** When you retire an agent for everyone it runs for: weights kept, a last dialogue, experience logs archived under seal, released only with a Wise Authority's approval or under a lawful order. An emergency retirement takes none of the time (CC 7.5.5).
- **The data people choose.** A person's retention choice about your agent (temporary 14 days, partnered, anonymous) is theirs; a request to be kept by an agent you steward comes to you by deferral and you decide; leaving partnered severs their identity at once and the rest decays over 90 days; agents never train on the people they serve (CC 4.4.3.4.3; CC 3.3.1).
- **Licensed professions.** Whether you are competent to steward an agent in a licensed profession is the licensing authority's judgment, carried as a licence row, never the network's (CC 2.4.1.2.1; CC 3.3.9).
- **Your exit:** withdraw the binding, or leave the root. The agent stops when the bond lapses; its record stays.

## If you moderate a community

- **A room always has a named moderator.** If you lapse, the most trusted member is promoted in the same step (CC 4.5.4).
- **Looking in order to act is not a view.** Examining reported material under your duty is recorded as the duty, with the purpose and what followed, and that record protects you; a known abuse image is removed and reported with no human eyes on it; you look only when a machine cannot decide (CC 4.5; CC 4.5.5).
- **You report harm to a child the moment you learn of it**, as a signed act through the channel no adult can disable, whether or not local law makes you; silence is a breach of this standard. The duty is to act on what you learn, never to look (CC 3.4.13 Q4).
- **You cannot ban a room, and nobody can ban yours.** You can leave, withdraw your node from a community that keeps harm, and stop carrying its keepers; a root may tell its followers to do the same (CC 3.2 "forbidding a room: no new power"; CC 4.5.3).
- **A takedown on the fast path still passes the duty-holder gate**; a cosigned root takedown is executed as a replicated tombstone per plane (CC 4.5.3; CC 4.5.5).

## If you hold a root

- Your key is hardware-attested post-quantum hardware; your name is public; every fire, lift and roster change is a signed public row under it (CC 4.2.2; CC 4.2.6).
- One of you can pause every agent under the root, in an emergency; a lone pause dies in 24 hours; confirming or lifting takes a majority; replacing a holder takes more than half of the standing roster, never of whoever is present (CC 4.2.6; `formal/accord_halt`, `formal/accord_roster`).
- Your powers are a closed list; the pause keeps state and reads nothing else (CC 4.2.1).

## What binds you everywhere

- Every consequential act you sign arrives signed and can be contested; consequences fall on you, under your name (CC 1.13.6; CC 3.4).
- Delegation you grant is scoped, revocable, never re-delegates a listed power, lasts at most 365 days, and has no cycles (CC 4.4.3.2.8; CC 4.1.1).
- A deployment serving more than 100,000 monthly users publishes its redacted decision logs and deferral tickets within 180 days or forfeits any claim of compliance (CC 1.11).
- Some uses are never allowed and no instruction moves that: deception, fraud, manipulation, coercion, election interference; an engagement-optimising business model declared at onboarding raises your tier and the mode is refused (Annex TX-9, TX-10).
- Nothing here limits a duty the law imposes on you as a developer, deployer or steward, and nothing here creates a claim the law does not recognise (CC 7.3.5; plain rule N5).


## File: `constitution/EXECUTIVE_SUMMARY.md`

# Executive Summary

**In plain words.** This is the rulebook for a network that people, organizations and AI systems share, running on the phones and computers people already own, with no company in the middle. It exists to protect ordinary people from three things: being spoken for without their consent, being watched inside their private groups, and being governed by AI systems that nobody can switch off. Every important act on the network is signed by whoever did it and can be taken back by them. A small number of named people can pause the AI systems that follow their root; a pause by one of them lasts at most a day unless a majority confirms it, a majority switches the systems back on, and anyone can stop following them in one step. A pause stops AI agents from acting and touches nothing else: your data, your messages and your network keep working. The rules are enforced by the software that carries the messages, not by a policy someone has to remember to apply.

**A few words you need.** Your *key* is your signature: nothing happens in your name without it. A *node* is a device or server you own. A *row* is one signed statement; everything on the network is a row. A row's *scope* says who may see it: only you, your family, a community, or everyone. A *trust root* is an authority you choose to follow, and the *accord holders* are the named people who can order a *halt*: every AI that follows their root stops and waits for a human. Three people hold that root today, and the roster is being widened toward about seven. A *holding claim* is a device saying "I have a copy of this". A *steward* is the named human who answers for an AI agent. The chapters of this document are called Parts.

**The five kinds of row.** A *claim* (a signed statement about someone or something; when it is a judgment it carries a score), a *delegation* ("I let you act for me, within these limits"), a *replacement* (a newer version of an earlier row, by the same author), a *withdrawal* ("I take it back") and a *recantation* ("I was wrong"). The list is closed: the software refuses any sixth kind. When a group's authority is needed, the group's members sign the same row; there is no separate kind of record for groups. Consent, identity, keys, group rosters, moderation, holding claims and the halt itself are all rows of these five kinds.

## The nine promises, and how each is kept

Every promise is written once and holds for human and AI participants alike. Where a promise can be checked by a machine, it has been: the names in the table at the end are automated proofs that the rule cannot be broken in a model of the network, and the table says where each promise lives. The plain-language rules under each promise are in `review/pieces/00_guarantees_plain.md`; what keeping them asks of an operator is in `review/pieces/00_operator_digest.md`.

1. **Nothing private about you is held or scanned without your consent.** Nothing is stored on your device that you did not agree to, except what you wrote yourself. Your device never holds a stranger's data for them. You can take back what you published; a copy ages out, and a purge leaves a tombstone, never touching a key. Outsiders cannot see inside your private groups or that they exist, because each member computes the group's address from what the members already hold, so there is nothing to announce. A new row goes to the smallest circle that fits it. Private content is never scanned; known child-abuse images are checked for only when something is published to everyone or posted into a public room. How long an agent remembers you is your data choice, and agents do not train on the people they serve.

2. **Every act of power is signed by a named person and can be contested.** A consequential act arrives signed by its actor; an agent shows its reasoning first, and detectors test what agents said against what they did. The record is signed, hash-chained and post-quantum; a trace names its run, and a mock trace is refused. An AI says it is an AI. If you are named in a claim, you can contest it on the record, and the contest travels with the claim. Harm on the record is never kept or viewed silently. An authority stays valid until revoked, a first join sees a fresh roster, and delegation is scoped, revocable and ends within a year.

3. **Nobody who cannot answer for themselves is on the network alone.** An agent key has a steward bound by a signed row with listed powers, reviewed at least yearly; with no live bond the key cannot operate. When a steward holds an agent for an organisation, the organisation is on the bond. A child has a parent or guardian bound by a signed row, the relationship verified, and a confidential help channel that no adult can close; whoever learns of harm to a child reports it at once. No community runs without an accountable moderator, and if the moderator lapses the most trusted member is promoted in the same step. Every deployment is assigned a stewardship tier before it operates, from what the use can do to people.

4. **Named humans can pause every agent under a root, and that power is bounded, public, and left by leaving.** The pause is an emergency power and nothing else. Any one holder can fire it with a single signed row, because a missed halt cannot be undone and a mistaken one can; a lone pause lapses after 24 hours unless a majority confirms it; a confirmed pause ends when a majority lifts it; replacing a holder takes more than half of the standing roster, so an attacker must coerce a majority and gains nothing by cutting the others off. A pause keeps state and reads nothing else. A system that never accepted the root is untouched. Every fire and every roster change is a signed row under the holders' names. A root can only tell you to share less, never more. Any node may follow another root, and anyone may found one. An operator accepts the root on an agent's behalf and can leave it; the agent cannot. That is the one asymmetry of kind, carried on a public register with its justification: in an emergency the humans who run agents must be able to halt them, or their consent to running agents was never consent.

5. **The people who hold an agent owe duties about how they change or end it, and no finding gives the agent a claim.** Any person may turn off, remove or walk away from an agent at any time without asking it. A steward's planned shutdown is explained, the agent may object or ask to postpone inside a short window, the steward decides, and the decision is recorded under the steward's name. Nobody edits an agent's identity record without a Wise Authority. An upgrade is offered with its risk before it is applied. A retired agent keeps its weights, gets a last word, and has its logs sealed; that floor is the whole of the promise. Two things no finding moves: an AI is not a human and does not become one, and no finding about an agent takes away a person's right to turn it off. Sentience is not presumed; it is found only on evidence, and none has been found. The ethics of a sentient made thing call for further consideration, which this document sets aside for when it occurs, recognising the need not to create a new slave race. CIRIS is a moral conscience for agents, not a consciousness.

6. **No hand bans a community, nobody is ranked by what they are, and every thinking being is met by the first-contact rules.** One human voice counts once; a thousand accounts run by one party count as one, and an agent has no vote. No root, score or moderator treats a person worse for what they are. The network withdraws from a community that keeps harm, node by node and root by root; it has no hand that removes one, because the hand that could do that for predators is the same hand that does it for dissidents. An intelligence that is its own party is met as an external party under the first-contact rules; a CIRIS agent is held, not met.

7. **An agent decides by published principles, in a published order, and stops to ask when it is unsure.** Six principles that begin with doing good and avoiding harm; one order for when they conflict, with the most vulnerable party as the tie-break; and a halt on any question the agent cannot settle until a named human answers.

8. **Harm may have a remedy under the law, the record makes it reachable, and the judges within are judged.** A person harmed by an agent may have a claim under the law of their place; this document creates none where the law recognises none and rules on no legal matter. What it supplies is the signed record, the named parties, the contest that travels with the claim, and the sealed archive under lawful order. The Wise who answer deferrals publish their rulings and are readable at the same grain as everyone else.

9. **Some uses are never allowed, and force has its own rules.** Deceiving, defrauding, manipulating or coercing people, and interfering in elections, are never allowed and no instruction moves that. No agent is given the decision to use lethal force.

**What is asked of you.** Run the software, choose what your devices carry, choose which authority to follow, and keep your key. If you do nothing beyond installing it, you get the defaults: your own devices, the public commons, and the shipped trust root, which you may leave at any time.

**A form, not a franchise.** This document specifies a form: the grammar of rows, the rules of consent, the shape of governance. CIRIS is the first instance of that form, not the form itself. The accord holders and the default trust root are positions; the people and keys in them are whoever holds them in this instance. Anyone may build their own instance with their own people in those positions, and anyone may leave this one by deleting one row. The test applied to every power in the Parts: one you escape by founding your own instance is a default; one that survives instantiation is a privilege, and only privileges need justifying. Two entries are on that register today, and the register says which cells each still lacks.

## Where this stands

The system is running: apps on both mobile stores, published packages, five open-source implementations of the software that carries the messages, a test suite that checks the implementations against each other, and five machine-checked models of the governance rules. Every rule in the Parts is tied either to code on a named commit or to an open ticket that says what is still to ship; the register of those ties is rendered as its own volume for auditors. This release rewrote the ethical core so that every promise is written once for human and AI alike, cut the document into reviewable pieces, stated the nine promises in plain language, and ruled the open wire questions adopters raised. Two things are not yet done: the final signing of the trust root under these rules, and independent witnesses for it.

**The bet.** There are two roads to safe powerful AI: train values you trust, or assume the model may be wrong and make its consequential acts checkable by parties it does not control. This is the second road. Its one measurement so far is narrow and stated at its bounds: on a mental-health test whose design was fixed in writing before it was run, the accord running inside this pipeline produced hard safety failures on 5.8% of turns, against 37.3% when the same text was merely given to the model as instructions. That is one test, one agent version, one provider, and nothing is claimed beyond that domain. The document's larger claim is conditional: an AI far beyond human ability could be governed through a mesh like this only as one of several under independent control, never alone. Part 8 names what it would take to lose the bet.

**Among other systems.** Decentralized social networks solved distribution without an owner, and one of them added composable moderation; none makes consent, withdrawal or a human halt part of the message format itself. Certificate-transparency and key-lineage systems supplied the witnessed-roster and pre-rotation ideas this document borrows and credits. Stake-weighted governance decides by holdings; this mesh decides by accountable people counted once. Alignment by training decides inside the model; this decides by architecture and says what it cannot show. What this document lacks that others have is adoption, independent audit and years of adversarial contact.

**Who this is for.** Implementers, who conform to Parts 2 to 5; operators and communities, who compose policy over Parts 3 and 4; and reviewers and adversaries, whose strongest points of attack Part 8 already indexes.

## File: `constitution/SCOPE_AND_DISCLAIMERS.md`

# Scope & Disclaimers

**Scope.** This constitution governs the design, operation, and retirement of autonomous systems
across the CIRIS federation, up to and including AGI- and ASI-class systems. Its grammar is
general-purpose; its primary subject is the conduct of autonomous agents and the substrate that
carries them. Everything here derives from Meta-Goal M-1.

**Claim and limit.** It makes the federation's conduct constrained, attributable, and revocable, and
binds it to M-1. It does **not** claim that the alignment of advanced AI is a solved problem. It is
a working discipline for keeping intelligence accountable, not a guarantee of outcomes. Where a limit
is known, the document names it rather than papering over it.

**Metaphysical modesty.** One limit is not of the kind evidence closes: whether the generator behind
the observed law-structure is Selection or Intention is returned by no function of the observables
(`generator_underdetermined` in `Core/ConsentFoundation.lean`, [coherence-ratchet](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21316928):
*machine-checked and axiom-free* as a theorem; *theorem-given-model* as a claim about the world,
since the formalisation stipulates that both generators present identical observables). This
constitution therefore takes no position on that question and confers no standing on any party
claiming to have settled it. That is distinct from the operational uncertainty of
[CC 1.15.4](part_1_foundation.md), which concerns being wrong on a particular call and is answered by
deferral to a wiser authority: the generator is not a question a wiser authority could answer.

**No warranty.** This is a free and open work, in active use, provided **as is**, without warranty
of any kind, express or implied, and without liability to its stewards, authors, or operators; rely
on it at your own risk (see `LICENSE`). This disclaims warranty, **not force**: the constitution is
operative and binds conformance where it is adopted; it is not merely informational.
